The objective of this research was to examine bioactive peptides derived from whey, focusing on their functional properties and potential applications in food and therapeutics. The research began with a bibliometric analysis, mapping scientific progress and research trends related to these peptides, particularly in key areas such as antioxidant and antihypertensive activities.

The antioxidant activity of whey-derived bioactive peptides is of particular interest as it helps neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reduce oxidative stress, a key factor in preventing chronic diseases such as cardiovascular diseases, type 2 diabetes, and cancer [7, 8]. ROS are metabolic byproducts that can cause significant damage to cellular structures, including membranes, lipids, proteins, and DNA. To mitigate these effects, living organisms possess endogenous antioxidant systems, but dietary supplementation with antioxidants, such as whey-derived bioactive peptides, can enhance this defense [9]. Furthermore, recent studies indicate that peptides derived from milk fermentation exhibit high antioxidant stability following in vitro digestion, demonstrating greater bioavailability of relevant bioactive compounds [10].
For example, the peptide β-lactoglobulin (β-LG) fragment f42–46 (Tyr–Val–Glu–Glu–Leu) has been shown to be more effective in scavenging radicals than an equimolar mixture of the same amino acids, suggesting that peptide structural integrity enhances antioxidant activity. The mechanisms of action include free radical scavenging, sulfhydryl group synergy, and iron chelation.
